implementation_notes: Swift makes the debug/production split explicit with two stdlib functions: assert(_:) is evaluated only in debug builds and disappears in -O, while precondition(_:) is checked in both debug and release and traps in release (it is skipped only under -Ounchecked); assertionFailure()/preconditionFailure() express the same for conditions discovered structurally. Both terminate the process - Swift offers no recoverable assertion exception - so rules that callers can violate belong in thrown errors or failable initializers instead, and the classic structure collapses into these calls plus a private invariant-checking method.
pitfalls: In -Ounchecked builds the optimizer may assume a precondition holds, so a violated precondition is undefined behaviour rather than a trap.
precondition traps even in release: using it on user-supplied input turns a bad request into a crashed app.
Neither function is catchable, so an invariant violation in a background task takes down the process; tests must exercise the same code path rather than expect a thrown error.
The message closure is only evaluated on failure, but the condition is evaluated whenever the check is active, so expensive predicates still cost in debug and preconditions also cost in release.
